facts.statement: Tyrannosaurus lived in western North America on the island continent of Laramidia during the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: It lived throughout what is now western North America, on what was then an island continent known as Laramidia.

facts.statement: Fossils of Tyrannosaurus date to the late Maastrichtian age, between 69 and 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Fossils are found in geological formations which have been dated to the late Maastrichtian age of the late Cretaceous period, 69 to 66 million years ago

facts.statement: Tyrannosaurus had short but unusually powerful forelimbs with two clawed digits relative to its large hind limbs.
facts.quote: Relative to its large and powerful hind limbs, the forelimbs of Tyrannosaurus were short but unusually powerful for their size, and they had two clawed digits.

facts.statement: While the most complete specimen is 12.3 to 12.4 meters long, modern estimates suggest Tyrannosaurus could reach 13 meters in length, 3.7 to 4 meters in height, and 8.8 tons in mass.
facts.quote: The most complete specimen measures 12.3 - 12.4 m in length, but according to most modern estimates, Tyrannosaurus could have exceeded sizes of 13 m in length, 3.7 - 4 m in hip height, and 8.8 t in mass.

facts.statement: Tyrannosaurus had the largest estimated bite force of any terrestrial animal.
facts.quote: it is still among the largest known land predators, with its estimated bite force being the largest among all terrestrial animals.

facts.statement: Tyrannosaurus was likely an apex predator that preyed on hadrosaurs, juvenile ceratopsians, ankylosaurs, and possibly sauropods.
facts.quote: By far the largest carnivore in its environment, Tyrannosaurus rex was most likely an apex predator, preying upon hadrosaurs, juvenile armored herbivores like ceratopsians and ankylosaurs, and possibly sauropods.

facts.statement: Scientists have debated whether Tyrannosaurus was primarily an apex predator or a scavenger.
facts.quote: The question of whether Tyrannosaurus was an apex predator or a pure scavenger was among the longest debates in paleontology.

facts.statement: A tooth identified as Tyrannosaurus rex was found in July 1874 near Golden, Colorado, by Peter T. Dotson.
facts.quote: A tooth from what is now documented as a Tyrannosaurus rex was found in July 1874 upon South Table Mountain (Colorado) by Jarvis Hall student Peter T. Dotson under the auspices of Arthur Lakes near Golden, Colorado

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope named a large dinosaur with two vertebral fragments Manospondylus gigas in 1892, initially believing it to be a ceratopsid.
facts.quote: In 1892, Edward Drinker Cope found two vertebral fragments of a large dinosaur. Cope believed the fragments belonged to an "agathaumid" (ceratopsid) dinosaur, and named them Manospondylus gigas

facts.statement: Barnum Brown discovered the first partial skeleton of Tyrannosaurus rex in eastern Wyoming in 1900.
facts.quote: Barnum Brown, assistant curator of the American Museum of Natural History, found the first partial skeleton of T. rex in eastern Wyoming in 1900.

facts.statement: Henry Fairfield Osborn named the second Tyrannosaurus skeleton T. rex in 1905.
facts.quote: Henry Fairfield Osborn, president of the American Museum of Natural History, named the second skeleton T. rex in 1905.

facts.statement: The genus Tyrannosaurus was described by Osborn in 1905.
facts.quote: authority: Osborn, 1905

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Tyrannosaurus is Tyrannosaurus rex.
facts.quote: type_species: Tyrannosaurus rex

facts.statement: T. mcraeensis is a proposed species of Tyrannosaurus described by Dalman et al. in 2024.
facts.quote: subdivision: * T. mcraeensis? Dalman et al., 2024 See text

facts.statement: The validity of recently discovered species like T. mcraeensis is a subject of debate.
facts.quote: The validity of these species, such as the more recently discovered T. mcraeensis, is contentious.

facts.statement: Osborn named the first Tyrannosaurus skeleton Dynamosaurus imperiosus in 1905.
facts.quote: Osborn named the other specimen Dynamosaurus imperiosus in a 1905 paper.

facts.statement: Osborn recognized that the two skeletons were the same species and chose Tyrannosaurus as the valid name in 1906.
facts.quote: In 1906, Osborn recognized that the two skeletons were from the same species and selected Tyrannosaurus as the preferred name.

facts.statement: Starting in the 1960s, renewed interest led to the recovery of 42 Tyrannosaurus skeletons from western North America, ranging from 5% to 80% completeness by bone count.
facts.quote: Beginning in the 1960s, there was renewed interest in Tyrannosaurus, resulting in the recovery of 42 skeletons (5–80% complete by bone count) from western North America.

facts.statement: Sue Hendrickson discovered the largest and most complete Tyrannosaurus skeleton, approximately 85% complete, in the Hell Creek Formation on August 12, 1990.
facts.quote: Sue Hendrickson discovered the most complete (approximately 85%) and largest Tyrannosaurus skeleton in the Hell Creek Formation on August 12, 1990.

facts.statement: In 1998, 20-year-old Bucky Derflinger became the youngest person to discover a Tyrannosaurus by finding an exposed toe.
facts.quote: In 1998, 20-year-old Bucky Derflinger noticed a T. rex toe exposed above ground, making him the youngest person to discover a Tyrannosaurus.

facts.statement: The Bucky specimen was a young adult Tyrannosaurus measuring 10 feet tall and 35 feet long.
facts.quote: The specimen, dubbed Bucky in honor of its discoverer, was a young adult, 10 ft tall and 35 ft long.

facts.statement: Bucky is the first Tyrannosaurus specimen found to preserve a furcula, or wishbone.
facts.quote: Bucky is the first Tyrannosaurus to be found that preserved a furcula (wishbone).

facts.statement: In 2001, a crew from the Burpee Museum of Natural History discovered a 50% complete juvenile Tyrannosaurus skeleton in the Hell Creek Formation.
facts.quote: In 2001, a 50% complete skeleton of a juvenile Tyrannosaurus was discovered in the Hell Creek Formation by a crew from the Burpee Museum of Natural History.

facts.statement: The juvenile skeleton 'Jane' was initially debated as either a pygmy tyrannosaurid or a juvenile T. rex, but is now re-described as the holotype of Nanotyrannus lethaeus.
facts.quote: Dubbed Jane (BMRP 2002.4.1), the find was thought to be the first known skeleton of a pygmy tyrannosaurid, Nanotyrannus, but other researchers considered it as the most complete juvenile T. rex; currently exhibited at the Burpee Museum of Natural History, Jane is now re-described as the holotype of N. lethaeus.

facts.statement: In 2006, Montana State University revealed it possessed the largest Tyrannosaurus skull discovered, measuring 5 feet long.
facts.quote: In 2006, Montana State University revealed that it possessed the largest Tyrannosaurus skull yet discovered (from a specimen named MOR 008), measuring 5 ft long.

facts.statement: Comparisons indicate the longest Tyrannosaurus head measured 136.5 cm and the widest measured 90.2 cm.
facts.quote: Subsequent comparisons indicated that the longest head was 136.5 cm (from specimen LACM 23844) and the widest head was 90.2 cm (from Sue).

facts.statement: The Sue specimen measured 12.3 to 12.8 meters long, 3.66 to 3.96 meters tall at the hips, with estimated maximum body masses between 8.4 and 9.22 metric tons.
facts.quote: One of its largest and the most complete specimens, Sue (FMNH PR2081), measured 12.3 - 12.8 m long, was 3.66 - 3.96 m tall at the hips, and according to the most recent studies, using a variety of techniques, maximum body masses have been estimated approximately 8.4 - 9.22 MT.

facts.statement: The Scotty specimen is reported to measure 13 meters in length.
facts.quote: A specimen nicknamed Scotty (RSM P2523.8), located at the Royal Saskatchewan Museum, is reported to measure 13 m in length.

facts.statement: Based on femur circumference, the Scotty specimen was estimated to have a body mass of 8.87 metric tons, making it the largest known specimen by mass.
facts.quote: Using a mass estimation technique that extrapolates from the circumference of the femur, Scotty was estimated as the largest known specimen at 8.87 MT in body mass.

facts.statement: Historical mass estimates for adult Tyrannosaurus varied from 4.5 to over 7.2 metric tons, while modern estimates typically range between 5.4 and 8.0 metric tons.
facts.quote: Historically average adult mass estimates have varied widely over the years, from as low as 4.5 MT, to more than 7.2 MT, with most modern estimates ranging between 5.4 and 8.0 MT.

facts.statement: A 2024 study found little evidence for size-based sexual dimorphism in Tyrannosaurus rex.
facts.quote: A 2024 study found that there was little evidence of size-based sexual dimorphism in T. rex.

facts.statement: The largest known Tyrannosaurus skulls measure up to 1.52 meters in length.
facts.quote: The largest known T. rex skulls measure up to 1.52 m in length.

facts.statement: The Tyrannosaurus skull was extremely wide at the rear with a narrow snout, providing unusually good binocular vision.
facts.quote: It was extremely wide at the rear but had a narrow snout, allowing unusually good binocular vision.

facts.statement: Skull-strengthening features in Tyrannosaurus contributed to a bite force that surpassed all non-tyrannosaurid dinosaurs.
facts.quote: These and other skull-strengthening features are part of the tyrannosaurid trend towards an increasingly powerful bite, which easily surpassed that of all non-tyrannosaurids.

facts.statement: The U-shaped tip of the Tyrannosaurus upper jaw allowed it to rip out more tissue and bone in one bite compared to V-shaped jaws, though this increased stress on the front teeth.
facts.quote: The tip of the upper jaw was U-shaped (most non-tyrannosauroid carnivores had V-shaped upper jaws), which increased the amount of tissue and bone a tyrannosaur could rip out with one bite, although it also increased the stresses on the front teeth.

facts.statement: The largest Tyrannosaurus tooth found so far was estimated to be 30.5 cm long including the root, making it the largest tooth of any known carnivorous dinosaur.
facts.quote: The largest found so far is estimated to have been 30.5 cm long including the root when the animal was alive, making it the largest tooth of any carnivorous dinosaur yet found.

facts.statement: Researchers have debated the function of holes in the Tyrannosaurus jaws, proposing they served as a sensory system or supported extra-oral structures like lips, with some research supporting the latter.
facts.quote: Various functions have been proposed for these foramina, such as a crocodile-like sensory system or evidence of extra-oral structures such as scales or potentially lips, with subsequent research on theropod tooth wear patterns supporting such a proposition.

facts.statement: The number of tail vertebrae in T. rex is unknown but likely numbered at least forty.
facts.quote: The number of tail vertebrae is unknown and could well have varied between individuals but probably numbered at least forty.

facts.statement: The famous specimen 'Sue' was mounted with forty-seven tail vertebrae.
facts.quote: Sue was mounted with forty-seven of such caudal vertebrae.

facts.statement: The T. rex neck formed an S-shaped curve similar to other theropods.
facts.quote: The neck of T. rex formed a natural S-shaped curve like that of other theropods.

facts.statement: T. rex vertebral bodies featured single pleurocoels, which are pneumatic depressions created by air sacs.
facts.quote: The vertebral bodies had single pleurocoels, pneumatic depressions created by air sacs, on their sides.

facts.statement: The T. rex tail was heavy and moderately long to balance its massive head and torso and to house large locomotor muscles.
facts.quote: The tail was heavy and moderately long, in order to balance the massive head and torso and to provide space for massive locomotor muscles that attached to the thighbones.

facts.statement: The T. rex forelimb was very short.
facts.quote: The forelimb or arm was very short.

facts.statement: T. rex forelimbs had only two clawed fingers and a small splint-like third metacarpal representing a remnant digit.
facts.quote: The forelimbs had only two clawed fingers, along with an additional splint-like small third metacarpal representing the remnant of a third digit.

facts.statement: Many T. rex bones were hollowed to reduce weight without losing strength, compensating for the animal's immense bulk.
facts.quote: Compensating for the immense bulk of the animal, many bones throughout the skeleton were hollowed, reducing its weight without significant loss of strength.

facts.statement: Daspletosaurus and Tarbosaurus are other members of the tyrannosaurine subfamily and have occasionally been synonymized with Tyrannosaurus.
facts.quote: Other members of the tyrannosaurine subfamily include the North American Daspletosaurus and the Asian Tarbosaurus, both of which have occasionally been synonymized with Tyrannosaurus.

facts.statement: Tyrannosaurids were once thought to descend from megalosaurs and carnosaurs but were later reclassified with the smaller coelurosaurs.
facts.quote: Tyrannosaurids were once commonly thought to be descendants of earlier large theropods such as megalosaurs and carnosaurs, although more recently they were reclassified with the generally smaller coelurosaurs.

facts.statement: Many phylogenetic analyses identify Tarbosaurus bataar as the sister taxon of T. rex.
facts.quote: Many phylogenetic analyses have found Tarbosaurus bataar to be the sister taxon of T. rex.

facts.statement: A 2016 study suggests T. rex may have been an immigrant from Asia and a possible descendant of Tarbosaurus.
facts.quote: A further study from 2016 by Steve Brusatte, Thomas Carr and colleagues, also indicates that Tyrannosaurus may have been an immigrant from Asia, as well as a possible descendant of Tarbosaurus.

facts.statement: Tyrannosaurs began as small theropods, with at least some becoming larger by the Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Tyrannosaurs started out as small theropods; at least some became larger by the Early Cretaceous.

facts.statement: A juvenile Tyrannosaurus specimen known as the Jordan theropod weighed approximately 30 kg.
facts.quote: The Stygivenator holotype (LACM 28471, the "Jordan theropod"), possibly a juvenile T. rex, is estimated to have weighed only 30 kg

facts.statement: The largest adult Tyrannosaurus specimens, such as Sue, likely weighed about 5,650 kg.
facts.quote: the largest adults, such as FMNH PR2081 (Sue) most likely weighed about 5650 kg

facts.statement: Histological analysis revealed that the juvenile Jordan theropod was only 2 years old when it died.
facts.quote: Histologic analysis of T. rex bones showed LACM 28471 had aged only 2 years when it died

facts.statement: Recent studies estimate the age of the famous specimen Sue to be between 27 and 33 years.
facts.quote: Sue was initially estimated at 28 years old, an age which was at the time considered close to the maximum for the species, but the most recent studies estimate Sue's age at 27–33 years

facts.statement: The specimen Trix was estimated to be at least 30 years old at the time of its death.
facts.quote: Trix (RGM 792.000) is estimated to have been at least 30 years old at time of death

facts.statement: Juvenile Tyrannosaurus remained under 1,800 kg until they reached approximately 14 years of age.
facts.quote: A T. rex growth curve is S-shaped, with juveniles remaining under 1800 kg until approximately 14 years of age

facts.statement: During its rapid growth phase, a young Tyrannosaurus gained an average of 600 kg per year for four years.
facts.quote: During this rapid growth phase, a young T. rex would gain an average of 600 kg a year for the next four years

facts.statement: Growth in Tyrannosaurus slowed dramatically after reaching 18 years of age.
facts.quote: At 18 years of age, the curve plateaus again, indicating that growth slowed dramatically

facts.statement: A 2004 study found that rapid growth in Tyrannosaurus began to slow around 16 years of age.
facts.quote: A 2004 histological study performed by different workers corroborates these results, finding that rapid growth began to slow at around 16 years of age

facts.statement: A 2011 study estimated the maximum growth rate of Tyrannosaurus during its exponential stage to be 1,790 kg per year.
facts.quote: A study by Hutchinson and colleagues in 2011 corroborated the previous estimation methods in general, but their estimation of peak growth rates is significantly higher; it found that the "maximum growth rates for T. rex during the exponential stage are 1790 kg/year"

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that a sudden change in growth rate indicates physical maturity, a hypothesis supported by medullary tissue found in a 16 to 20-year-old Tyrannosaurus from Montana.
facts.quote: The sudden change in growth rate at the end of the growth spurt may indicate physical maturity, a hypothesis which is supported by the discovery of medullary tissue in the femur of a 16 to 20-year-old T. rex from Montana (MOR 1125, also known as B-rex)

facts.statement: The presence of medullary tissue in the femur of the specimen B-rex indicates it was a female of reproductive age.
facts.quote: Medullary tissue is found only in female birds during ovulation, indicating that B-rex was of reproductive age

facts.statement: In 2016, researchers confirmed that the soft tissue in the femur of specimen MOR 1125 was medullary bone.
facts.quote: In 2016, it was finally confirmed by Mary Higby Schweitzer and Lindsay Zanno and colleagues that the soft tissue within the femur of MOR 1125 was medullary tissue

facts.statement: A 2020 study suggests that Tyrannosaurus could slow its growth to counter environmental factors like food scarcity.
facts.quote: An additional study published in 2020 by Woodward and colleagues, for the journal Science Advances indicates that during their growth from juvenile to adult, Tyrannosaurus was capable of slowing down its growth to counter environmental factors such as lack of food

facts.statement: A January 2026 analysis of 17 specimens argued that Tyrannosaurus reached its maximum size at around 35 to 40 years of age.
facts.quote: In January 2026, Woodward, Myhrvold and Horner performed a comprehensive histological analysis of 17 tyrannosaur specimens, and argued that Tyrannosaurus likely experienced a more gradual annual growth rate slope than indicated by earlier studies and evidence of a protracted subadult stage, reaching asymptotic size at around 35–40 years of age

facts.statement: Recent researchers note that inconsistencies in growth curves do not necessarily support the proposal that Nanotyrannus is a distinct taxon from Tyrannosaurus.
facts.quote: While they acknowledged the possibility of these ontogenetically immature specimens representing Nanotyrannus as suggested by Zanno and Napoli (2025), they noted that the inconsistencies of these specimens observed in the growth curve do not necessarily bear weight on the proposal that Nanotyrannus is a distinct taxon

facts.statement: A 2017 study found that a Tyrannosaurus specimen nicknamed Wyrex preserves patches of mosaic scales on its tail, hip, and neck.
facts.quote: A 2017 study reviewed known skin impressions of tyrannosaurids, including those of a Tyrannosaurus specimen nicknamed "Wyrex" (HMNS 2006.1743.01, formerly known as BHI 6230) which preserves patches of mosaic scales on the tail, hip, and neck

facts.statement: A 2016 abstract proposed that theropods like Tyrannosaurus had lips covering their upper teeth.
facts.quote: A conference abstract published in 2016 posited that theropods such as Tyrannosaurus had their upper teeth covered in lips, instead of bare teeth as seen in crocodilians

facts.statement: In 2023, researchers supported the idea that theropods had lips based on facial and jaw foramina patterns similar to modern monitor lizards.
facts.quote: In 2023, Cullen and colleagues supported the idea that theropods like tyrannosaurids had lips based on anatomical patterns, such as those of the foramina on their face and jaws, more similar to those of modern squamates such as monitor lizards or marine iguanas than those of modern crocodilians like alligators

facts.statement: Comparisons show that tyrannosaurid teeth had no significant wear, unlike the substantially worn teeth of modern crocodilians.
facts.quote: Comparison of the teeth of Daspletosaurus and American alligators shows that the enamel of tyrannosaurids had no significant wear and that the teeth of modern crocodilians were eroded on the labial side and were substantially worn

facts.statement: The historical depiction of Tyrannosaurus as a bipedal dinosaur dates from Joseph Leidy's 1865 reconstruction of Hadrosaurus.
facts.quote: This concept dates from Joseph Leidy's 1865 reconstruction of Hadrosaurus, the first to depict a dinosaur in a bipedal posture.

facts.statement: Henry Fairfield Osborn unveiled the first complete Tyrannosaurus skeleton in an upright pose in 1915.
facts.quote: In 1915, convinced that the creature stood upright, Henry Fairfield Osborn, former president of the American Museum of Natural History, further reinforced the notion in unveiling the first complete T. rex skeleton arranged this way.

facts.statement: Modern representations show Tyrannosaurus with its body parallel to the ground and its tail extended to balance the head.
facts.quote: Modern representations in museums, art, and film show T. rex with its body approximately parallel to the ground with the tail extended behind the body to balance the head.

facts.statement: Healed stress fractures in Tyrannosaurus forelimbs are debated as evidence either of uselessness or of functional use and injury.
facts.quote: Healed stress fractures in the forelimbs have been put forward both as evidence that the arms cannot have been very useful and as evidence that they were indeed used and acquired wounds, like the rest of the body.

facts.statement: Tyrannosaurus arms measure only 1 meter in length and are considered vestigial by some scholars.
facts.quote: T. rex arms are very small relative to overall body size, measuring only 1 m long, and some scholars have labelled them as vestigial.

facts.statement: The biceps brachii muscle of an adult Tyrannosaurus could lift 199 kg by itself.
facts.quote: The biceps brachii muscle of an adult T. rex was capable of lifting 199 kg by itself

facts.statement: Paleontologists Kenneth Carpenter and Matt Smith argued that Tyrannosaurus forelimbs were not useless and that the animal was not an obligate scavenger.
facts.quote: In the first detailed scientific description of Tyrannosaurus forelimbs, paleontologists Kenneth Carpenter and Matt Smith dismissed notions that the forelimbs were useless or that Tyrannosaurus was an obligate scavenger.

facts.statement: Padian (2022) hypothesized that the reduction of tyrannosaurid arms was a secondary adaptation to avoid injury during group feedings rather than serving a specific function.
facts.quote: Padian (2022) argued that the reduction of the arms in tyrannosaurids did not serve a particular function but was a secondary adaptation, stating that as tyrannosaurids developed larger and more powerful skulls and jaws, the arms got smaller to avoid being bitten or torn by other individuals, particularly during group feedings.

facts.statement: Padian dismissed the hypothesis that Tyrannosaurus arms were used as weapons for slashing prey, arguing it was based on incorrect size and motion estimates.
facts.quote: This was dismissed by Padian, who argued that Stanley based his conclusion on incorrectly estimated forelimb size and range of motion.

facts.statement: Some scientists argue that oxygen isotope ratios in Tyrannosaurus fossils may have been altered by diagenesis and do not represent ancient temperatures.
facts.quote: Other scientists have pointed out that the ratio of oxygen isotopes in the fossils today does not necessarily represent the same ratio in the distant past, and may have been altered during or after fossilization (diagenesis).

facts.statement: In 2022, Wiemann and colleagues used lipoxidation spectroscopy to show that Tyrannosaurus had an endothermic metabolism comparable to modern birds and higher than mammals.
facts.quote: In 2022, Wiemann and colleagues used a different approach—the spectroscopy of lipoxidation signals, which are byproducts of oxidative phosphorylation and correlate with metabolic rates—to show that various dinosaur genera including Tyrannosaurus had endothermic metabolisms, on par with that of modern birds and higher than that of mammals.

facts.statement: It is debated whether evidence of homeothermy in Tyrannosaurus implies endothermy, as gigantothermy may explain the thermoregulation.
facts.quote: Even if T. rex does exhibit evidence of homeothermy, it does not necessarily mean that it was endothermic. Such thermoregulation may also be explained by gigantothermy, as in some living sea turtles.

facts.statement: Isotopic analysis found Tyrannosaurus had a body temperature of 36.3 C ± 2.5 °C, suggesting an endothermic metabolism.
facts.quote: Isotopic analysis found T. rex had a body temperature of 36.3 C ± 2.5 °C, suggesting it had an endothermic metabolism.

facts.statement: Estimates for the maximum running speed of Tyrannosaurus vary widely, ranging from 4.5 m/s to 20 m/s, with most estimates clustering around 9 m/s.
facts.quote: Scientists have produced a wide range of possible maximum running speeds for Tyrannosaurus: mostly around 9 m/s, but as low as 4.5 – 6.8 m/s and as high as 20 m/s.

facts.statement: Top speeds exceeding 40 km/h are considered infeasible for Tyrannosaurus because they would require leg muscles comprising 40% to 86% of its total body mass.
facts.quote: Proposed top speeds exceeded 40 km/h for Tyrannosaurus, but were deemed infeasible because they would require exceptional leg muscles of approximately 40–86% of total body mass.

facts.statement: If Tyrannosaurus possessed less leg muscle mass, its maximum speed would have been limited to 18 km/h, suitable only for walking or jogging.
facts.quote: If the muscle mass was less, only 18 km/h for walking or jogging would have been possible.

facts.statement: The arctometatarsus ankle feature in Tyrannosaurus may have helped the animal run more efficiently.
facts.quote: This ankle feature may have helped the animal to run more efficiently.

facts.statement: Researchers reconstructed muscles and ligaments in a 3-D model of the Tyrannosaurus specimen Trix to simulate tail movements during walking.
facts.quote: Using a 3-D model of Tyrannosaurus specimen Trix, muscles and ligaments were reconstructed to simulate the tail movements.

facts.statement: Simulations suggest Tyrannosaurus walked with a rhythmic, energy-efficient speed similar to that of modern humans, ostriches, and giraffes.
facts.quote: This results in a rhythmic, energy-efficient walking speed for Tyrannosaurus similar to that seen in living animals such as humans, ostriches and giraffes.

facts.statement: Evidence suggests that at least some tyrannosaurids, including Tyrannosaurus, hunted in group settings, drawing analogies to modern wolves.
facts.quote: Analogies can be noted between tyrannosaurids and modern wolves as a result, supported by evidence that at least some tyrannosaurids were hunting in group settings.

facts.statement: Studies suggest Tyrannosaurus had rapid and coordinated eye and head movements similar to other coelurosaurs.
facts.quote: A study conducted by Lawrence Witmer and Ryan Ridgely of Ohio University found that Tyrannosaurus shared the heightened sensory abilities of other coelurosaurs, highlighting relatively rapid and coordinated eye and head movements

facts.statement: Tyrannosaurus possessed an enhanced ability to sense low-frequency sounds, potentially allowing it to track prey from long distances.
facts.quote: an enhanced ability to sense low frequency sounds, which would allow tyrannosaurs to track prey movements from long distances

facts.statement: Tyrannosaurus had very large olfactory bulbs and nerves relative to its brain size, indicating a highly developed sense of smell.
facts.quote: Tyrannosaurus had very large olfactory bulbs and olfactory nerves relative to their brain size

facts.statement: A study speculated that tyrannosaurs used their sensitive snouts to measure nest temperatures and handle eggs and hatchlings.
facts.quote: The study speculated that tyrannosaurs might have used their sensitive snouts to measure the temperature of their nests and to gently pick up eggs and hatchlings

facts.statement: The discovery of three T. rex skeletons in close proximity in South Dakota suggests the possibility of pack formation.
facts.quote: A find in South Dakota where three T. rex skeletons were in close proximity may suggest the formation of a pack

facts.statement: Philip J. Currie hypothesized that T. rex was a pack hunter, a theory based on comparisons to related species like Tarbosaurus and Albertosaurus.
facts.quote: Philip J. Currie suggested that Tyrannosaurus may have been pack hunters, comparing T. rex to related species Tarbosaurus bataar and Albertosaurus sarcophagus

facts.statement: Currie's pack-hunting hypothesis has been criticized for lacking peer review and originating from a television interview and book.
facts.quote: Currie's pack-hunting T. rex hypothesis has been criticized for not having been peer-reviewed, but rather was discussed in a television interview and book called Dino Gangs

facts.statement: Some researchers speculate that evidence for social behavior in tyrannosaurs represents mobbing behavior similar to Komodo dragons rather than true pack hunting.
facts.quote: Others researchers have speculated that instead of large theropod social groups, some of these finds represent behavior more akin to Komodo dragon-like mobbing of carcasses

facts.statement: Pathologies in T. rex specimens, such as a hole in the jugal of 'Wyrex' and tail trauma, are suggested as evidence of attacks by other T. rex.
facts.quote: Pathologies of Tyrannosaurus specimens have been suggested as evidence of conspecific attack, including "Wyrex" with a hole penetrating its jugual and severe trauma on its tail

facts.statement: Chemical analysis of tooth enamel suggests Tyrannosaurus may have occasionally scavenged marine reptiles and fish washed ashore from the Western Interior Seaway.
facts.quote: Enamel δ44/42Ca values also suggest the possibility that T. rex occasionally fed on carcasses of marine reptiles and fish washed up on the shores of the Western Interior Seaway.

facts.statement: Researchers calculated that Tyrannosaurus could open its jaws up to 80 degrees to facilitate its powerful bite.
facts.quote: Stephan Lautenschlager and colleagues calculated that Tyrannosaurus was capable of a maximum jaw gape of around 80 degrees, a necessary adaptation for a wide range of jaw angles to power the creature's strong bite.

facts.statement: Fossil evidence includes at least one, and possibly two, Edmontosaurus specimens with healed tail injuries caused by living Tyrannosaurus attacks.
facts.quote: There is at least one and possibly two fossil specimens of the hadrosaur Edmontosaurus annectens with healed caudal injuries caused by Tyrannosaurus bites made while the herbivore was alive.

facts.statement: The fossil specimen 'Sue' shows healed injuries including a tooth from another Tyrannosaurus embedded in its neck vertebra, indicating aggressive interactions between individuals.
facts.quote: Studies of Sue found a broken and healed fibula and tail vertebrae, scarred facial bones and a tooth from another Tyrannosaurus embedded in a neck vertebra, providing evidence for aggressive behavior.

facts.statement: Paleontologist Jack Horner has argued that Tyrannosaurus was an obligate scavenger rather than a predator, a view supported by arguments regarding its short arms and sense of smell.
facts.quote: Paleontologist Jack Horner has been a major proponent of the view that Tyrannosaurus was not a predator at all but instead was an obligate scavenger.

facts.statement: Most evidence points to hunting behavior, supported by the forward-facing eye sockets that provided Tyrannosaurus with binocular vision superior to that of modern hawks.
facts.quote: Most evidence suggests hunting behavior in Tyrannosaurus. The eye sockets of tyrannosaurs are positioned so that the eyes would point forward, giving them binocular vision slightly better than that of modern hawks.

facts.statement: Research indicates that Tyrannosaurus possessed the most highly developed sense of smell among 21 sampled dinosaur species.
facts.quote: Research on the olfactory bulbs of dinosaurs has shown that Tyrannosaurus had the most highly developed sense of smell of 21 sampled dinosaurs.

facts.statement: Analysis of very young Tyrannosaurus specimens suggests that if parental care occurred, it was likely limited in scope.
facts.quote: Some very young specimens assigned to Tyrannosaurus rex suggest that, although the species may have provided parental care, it was likely limited.

facts.statement: Tendon avulsion injuries were found only in Tyrannosaurus and Allosaurus among the theropods studied.
facts.quote: The researchers found tendon avulsions only among Tyrannosaurus and Allosaurus.

facts.statement: Researchers concluded that the tendon avulsion injury found on the specimen 'Sue' was likely caused by struggling prey.
facts.quote: The researchers concluded that Sue's tendon avulsion was probably obtained from struggling prey.

facts.statement: Evidence of stress fractures and tendon avulsions suggests T. rex had a very active predation-based diet rather than being an obligate scavenger.
facts.quote: The presence of stress fractures and tendon avulsions, in general, provides evidence for a "very active" predation-based diet rather than obligate scavenging.

facts.statement: A 2009 study proposed that smooth-edged holes in T. rex skulls might have been caused by Trichomonas-like parasites, though this hypothesis was later challenged.
facts.quote: A 2009 study showed that smooth-edged holes in the skulls of several specimens might have been caused by Trichomonas-like parasites that commonly infect birds.

facts.statement: A later study suggested the skull lesions in T. rex resemble healing fractures or trepanations rather than infections, pointing to intraspecific combat as a possible cause.
facts.quote: A more recent study examining the pathologies concluded that the osseous alteration observed most closely resembles those around healing human cranial trepanations and healing fractures in the Triassic reptile Stagonolepis, in the absence of infection.

facts.statement: Tyrannosaurus rex is the type species of the genus Tyrannosaurus.
facts.quote: type_species: Tyrannosaurus rex

facts.statement: Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis was described as a valid species in 2024 by Dalman and colleagues.
facts.quote: subdivision: Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis Dalman et al., 2024

facts.statement: Several names, including Manospondylus and Dynamosaurus, have been used as synonyms for Tyrannosaurus.
facts.quote: synonyms: * Manospondylus Cope, 1892 Dynamosaurus Osborn, 1905 Stygivenator Olshevsky, 1995 Dinotyrannus Olshevsky, 1995

facts.statement: Tyrannosaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous, between 72 and 66 million years ago, in what is now North America.
facts.quote: que vivieron a finales del período Cretácico Superior, entre 72 a 66 millones de años, entre el Campaniense y el Maastrichtiense, en lo que es hoy América del Norte.

facts.statement: Tyrannosaurus was a bipedal carnivore with a huge head balanced by a long, heavy tail.
facts.quote: Tyrannosaurus fue un carnívoro bípedo con un enorme cráneo equilibrado por una cola larga y pesada.

facts.statement: T. rex had small but surprisingly strong forelimbs ending in two clawed fingers, contrasting with its long, powerful hind legs.
facts.quote: En relación con sus largos y poderosos miembros traseros, los miembros superiores de Tyrannosaurus eran pequeños, pero sorprendentemente fuertes para su tamaño, y terminaban en dos dedos con garras.

facts.statement: Specimens of T. rex measured between 11.1 and 13 meters long and weighed between 5.6 and 9.5 tonnes.
facts.quote: Distintos ejemplares hallados de Tyrannosaurus rex medían entre 11,1 y 13 metros de longitud, con pesos estimados de 5,6 a 9,5 toneladas.

facts.statement: T. rex possessed a large skull about 1.4 meters long with eye and nasal openings.
facts.quote: Tyrannosaurus poseía un gran cráneo de alrededor de 1,4 metros provisto de fenestras oculares y nasales.

facts.statement: The T. rex skull had many fused bones creating a solid structure, an unusual trait for theropods which typically had lightweight bones.
facts.quote: Su cráneo presenta un gran número de huesos fusionados, supliendo la movilidad por una estructura más maciza, hecho inusual en los terópodos, que por lo general tenían huesos ligeros.

facts.statement: The T. rex tail was long and heavy, formed by more than forty vertebrae, to balance its massive torso and head.
facts.quote: La cola era pesada y larga, formada por más de cuarenta vértebras, para equilibrar los enormes torso y cabeza.

facts.statement: Many T. rex bones were hollow to reduce weight without significantly losing strength.
facts.quote: Para compensar el inmenso tamaño del animal, muchos huesos de su esqueleto eran huecos, reduciendo su peso sin pérdida significativa de fuerza.

facts.statement: Teeth identified today as T. rex were found in 1874 by Arthur Lakes near Golden, Colorado.
facts.quote: Unos dientes que hoy son documentados como Tyrannosaurus rex fueron encontrados en 1874 por Arthur Lakes cerca de Golden, Colorado.

facts.statement: John Bell Hatcher collected postcranial elements of T. rex in eastern Wyoming in the early 1890s.
facts.quote: A principios de la década de 1890, John Bell Hatcher recolectó elementos postcraneales en el este de Wyoming.

facts.statement: Soft tissue and proteins have been found in at least one T. rex specimen.
facts.quote: Se han encontrado tejido conjuntivo y proteínas en por lo menos uno de estos especímenes.

facts.statement: Whether T. rex was a dominant predator or primarily a scavenger remains one of the longest debates in paleontology.
facts.quote: El debate de si Tyrannosaurus fue un depredador dominante o un carroñero es uno de los más largos en la paleontología.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope discovered two vertebral fragments of a large dinosaur in 1892, one of which is now lost.
facts.quote: En 1892, Edward Drinker Cope encontró dos fragmentos vertebrales, uno de los cuales se encuentra perdido, de un gran dinosaurio.

facts.statement: In 1907, Hatcher identified the remains of Manospondylus gigas as belonging to a theropod rather than a ceratopsian.
facts.quote: Los restos de M. gigas fueron, en 1907, identificados por Hatcher como los de un terópodo en lugar de un ceratópsido.

facts.statement: Henry Fairfield Osborn attributed Manospondylus gigas to Tyrannosaurus rex in 1912.
facts.quote: Fue atribuida a Tyrannosaurus rex en 1912 por Henry Fairfield Osborn.

facts.statement: In June 2000, a team from the Black Hills Institute located the site of M. gigas in South Dakota and unearthed about 10% of a Tyrannosaurus skeleton cataloged as BHI 6248.
facts.quote: En junio de 2000, un equipo del Instituto Black Hills localizó la ubicación de M.gigas en Dakota del Sur y desenterró nuevos huesos de alrededor del 10% de un esqueleto de Tyrannosaurus en dicho lugar, catalogados bajo el número BHI 6248.

facts.statement: Henry Fairfield Osborn, president of the American Museum of Natural History, described Tyrannosaurus rex to science in 1905.
facts.quote: Henry Fairfield Osborn, presidente del Museo Americano de Historia Natural, describió para la ciencia a Tyrannosaurus rex en 1905.

facts.statement: Barnum Brown found the first T. rex skeleton in Wyoming in 1900.
facts.quote: Barnum Brown, el conservador auxiliar del Museo Americano de Historia Natural, encontró el primer esqueleto de T.rex en Wyoming en 1900.

facts.statement: Barnum Brown found another partial skeleton in the Hell Creek Formation in Montana in 1902, comprising approximately 34 fossilized bones.
facts.quote: Luego encontró otro esqueleto parcial en la Formación Hell Creek en Montana, en 1902, que comprende aproximadamente 34 huesos fosilizados.

facts.statement: In 1906, Osborn recognized that the two skeletons belonged to the same species and selected Tyrannosaurus as the preferred name.
facts.quote: En 1906, Osborn reconoció que los dos esqueletos eran de la misma especie y seleccionó Tyrannosaurus como el nombre preferido.

facts.statement: In 1941, the T. rex type specimen was sold to the Carnegie Museum of Natural History in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, for 7,000 dollars.
facts.quote: En 1941, el espécimen tipo T. rex fue vendido al Museo Carnegie de Historia Natural en Pittsburgh, Pensilvania, por 7000 dólares.

facts.statement: In total, Barnum Brown found five partial T. rex skeletons.
facts.quote: En total, Barnum Brown encontró cinco esqueletos parciales de T.rex.

facts.statement: Brown's fourth and most important find, also discovered in the Hell Creek Formation, is displayed at the American Museum of Natural History in New York.
facts.quote: El cuarto hallazgo de Brown, que fue el más importante, también descubierto en la formación Hell Creek, está expuesto en el Museo Americano de Historia Natural en Nueva York.

facts.statement: In 2024, Dalman and colleagues described remains of a Tyrannosaurus discovered in 1983 in the Lake Hall Formation at the Campanian-Maastrichtian boundary in New Mexico, USA.
facts.quote: En 2024, Dalman y sus colegas describieron los restos de un Tyrannosaurus descubierto en 1983 en la Formación Lago Hall del límite Campaniense-Maastrichtiense en Nuevo México Estados Unidos.

facts.statement: In 2024, Dalman and colleagues proposed the new name Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis for the holotype NMMNH P-3698, referencing the McRae Group rock layers of the Lake Hall Formation.
facts.quote: Dalman y colegas en 2024 propusieron el nuevo nombre Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis para el holotipo, NMMNH P-3698, haciendo referencia al Grupo McRae, las capas de rocas a las que pertenece la Formación Lago Hall.

facts.statement: The rock layers are estimated to date between 72.7 and 70.9 million years ago, correlating with the late Campanian or early Maastrichtian.
facts.quote: Se estimó que estas capas de roca databan de entre 72,7 y 70,9 millones de años, lo que se correlaciona con el Campaniense tardío o el Maastrichtiense temprano.

facts.statement: This is approximately 5 to 7 million years before T. rex, which existed at the end of the last period.
facts.quote: Esto es aproximadamente entre 5 y 7 millones de años antes del T. rex, que existió a finales del último período.

facts.statement: T. mcraeensis is estimated to have measured 12 meters in length, similar to the size of an adult T. rex.
facts.quote: Se estimó que T. mcraeensis medía 12 metros de largo, lo que es similar al tamaño de un T. rex adulto.

facts.statement: The dentary of T. mcraeensis is proportionally longer with a less prominent chin and shallower lower jaw than T. rex, suggesting a weaker bite.
facts.quote: Entre estos, el dentario de T. mcraeensis es proporcionalmente más largo y posee un mentón menos prominente y la mandíbula inferior menos profunda que la del T. rex, lo que sugiere una mordida más débil.

facts.statement: The teeth are also blunter and more laterally compressed, while the postorbital crests are less prominent.
facts.quote: Los dientes también son más romos y más comprimidos lateralmente, mientras que las crestas postorbitarias son menos prominentes.

facts.statement: Due to the fragmented state of Manospondylus vertebrae, Osborn did not synonymize the two genera but considered the older genus indeterminate.
facts.quote: Debido al estado fragmentado de las vértebras de Manospondylus, Osborn no sinonimizó los dos géneros, sino que consideró indeterminado el género más antiguo.

facts.statement: According to the ICZN rules, Manospondylus should have had priority over Tyrannosaurus for being used first, which would also apply to the species.
facts.quote: De acuerdo con las reglas del Código Internacional de Nomenclatura Zoológica (ICZN), el sistema que gobierna los nombres científicos de los animales, Manospondylus debería haber tenido prioridad sobre Tyrannosaurus por haber sido utilizado primero, cosa que también sucederia con las especies.

facts.statement: However, the fourth edition of the ICZN, effective January 1, 2000, established an exception allowing Tyrannosaurus rex to remain the valid name.
facts.quote: Sin embargo la cuarta edición de la ICZN, que empezó a tener efecto el 1 de enero de 2000, estableció una excepción que permite seguir considerando Tyrannosaurus rex como el nombre válido.

facts.statement: If challenged before the ICZN, which has not yet occurred, Manospondylus gigas would likely be considered a nomen oblitum ('forgotten name') while Tyrannosaurus rex remains a nomen protectum ('protected name').
facts.quote: Si alguien lo desafiase ante la ICZN, cosa que todavía no ha ocurrido, muy probablemente sería considerado un nomen protectum, "nombre protegido", y Manospondylus gigas sería considerado nomen oblitum, "nombre olvidado".

facts.statement: The first specimen was originally named Dynamosaurus imperiosus in the same document where Tyrannosaurus rex was described from the second specimen.
facts.quote: El primer espécimen fue originalmente nombrado Dynamosaurus imperiosus en el mismo documento en el que fue descrito Tyrannosaurus rex a partir del segundo.

facts.statement: Dynamosaurus was later honored by the 2018 description of another tyrannosaurid species by Andrew McDonald and colleagues, Dynamoterror dynastes, named in reference to the 1905 name as it was a 'childhood favorite' of McDonald's.
facts.quote: Dynamosaurus, más tarde sería honrado por la descripción de 2018 de otra especie de tiranosáurido por Andrew McDonald y sus colegas, Dynamoterror dynastes, cuyo nombre se eligió en referencia al nombre de 1905, ya que había sido un "favorito de la infancia" de McDonald's.

facts.statement: Lehman and Carpenter suggested in 1990 that NMMNH P-3698 belonged to a new tyrannosaurid genus, while Carr and Williamson disagreed in 2000.
facts.quote: Lehman y Carpenter en 1990 sugirieron que NMMNH P-3698 pertenecía a un nuevo género de tiranosáuridos, mientras que Carr y Williamson en 2000 no estuvieron de acuerdo con su afirmación.

facts.statement: Sullivan and Lucas argued in 2015 that there is little evidence supporting NMMNH P-3698 as a T. rex specimen, so they tentatively classified it as cf. Tyrannosaurus sp.
facts.quote: Sullivan y Lucas en 2015 argumentaron que hay pocas pruebas que respalden a NMMNH P-3698 como un espécimen de Tyrannosaurus rex, por lo que lo clasificaron tentativamente como cf. Tyrannosaurus sp.

facts.statement: Dalman and colleagues proposed the new name Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis for the holotype NMMNH P-3698 in 2024.
facts.quote: Dalman y colegas en 2024 propusieron el nuevo nombre Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis para el holotipo, NMMNH P-3698, haciendo referencia al Grupo McRae, las capas de rocas a las que pertenece la Formación Lago Hall.

facts.statement: The skeletal anatomy shows shared characteristics with Tarbosaurus and Zhuchengtyrannus.
facts.quote: La anatomía esquelética muestra características compartidas con Tarbosaurus y Zhuchengtyrannus.

facts.statement: Cope believed the fragments belonged to a ceratopsian dinosaur and named them Manospondylus gigas, meaning 'giant porous vertebra', referring to numerous openings for blood vessels found in the bone.
facts.quote: Cope creía que los fragmentos pertenecían a un dinosaurio "agatáumido", ceratópsido, y los llamó Manospondylus gigas, que significa "vértebra porosa gigante", en referencia a las numerosas aberturas para los vasos sanguíneos que encontró en el hueso.

facts.statement: The generic name comes from Greek words tyrannos meaning 'tyrant' and sauros meaning 'lizard', while Osborn used the Latin word rex, meaning 'king', for the specific term.
facts.quote: El nombre genérico proviene de las palabras en griego τυραννος, tyrannos, que significa "tirano" y σαυρος, sauros, por "lagarto". Osborn usó la palabra latina rex, que se traduce como "rey", para el término específico.

facts.statement: The full binomial name Tyrannosaurus rex translates from Latin as 'king of the tyrant lizards', emphasizing the dinosaur's large size and supposed dominance over other animals of its time.
facts.quote: La nomenclatura binominal completa de esta especie, Tyrannosaurus rex, se traduce del latín como "el rey de los lagartos tiranos", poniendo énfasis en el gran tamaño del dinosaurio, con el que, se supone, dominaba a todos los otros animales de su tiempo.

facts.statement: It was the first and only species of the genus until 2024.
facts.quote: Siendo la primera especie y única del género hasta 2024.

facts.statement: It is debated whether NMMNH P-3698 belongs to T. rex, with some researchers arguing there is little evidence to support this classification.
facts.quote: Sullivan y Lucas en 2015 argumentaron que hay pocas pruebas que respalden a NMMNH P-3698 como un espécimen de Tyrannosaurus rex, por lo que lo clasificaron tentativamente como cf. Tyrannosaurus sp.

facts.statement: Researchers suggested that the so-called 'McRae tyrannosaur' lived before the Lancian, approximately 67 million years ago, based on its coexistence with Alamosaurus.
facts.quote: Sullivan y Lucas en 2015 argumentaron que hay pocas pruebas que respalden a NMMNH P-3698 como un espécimen de Tyrannosaurus rex, por lo que lo clasificaron tentativamente como cf. Tyrannosaurus sp. y también consideraron que el llamado por entonces "tiranosaurio de McRae" vivió antes del Lanciense, hace 67 millones de años, con base en su coexistencia con Alamosaurus.

facts.statement: Tyrannosaurus belongs to the parent group Tyrannosaurini.
facts.quote: Parent group: Tyrannosaurini

facts.statement: Tyrannosaurus is classified within the family Tyrannosauridae.
facts.quote: Family: Tyrannosauridae

facts.statement: Tyrannosaurus is classified as a reptile.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: Research suggests that Tyrannosaurus had a more gradual annual growth rate and a prolonged subadult stage than previously thought, with specific specimens not fitting earlier growth models.
facts.quote: Woodward, Myhrvold & Horner (2026) reconstruct the life history of Tyrannosaurus on the basis of bone histology, reporting evidence of a more gradual annual growth rate slope than indicated by earlier studies and evidence of a protracted subadult stage, and find that growth trajectories of the tyrannosaur specimens BMRP 2002.4.1 (the holotype of Nanotyrannus lethaeus) and BMRP 2006.4.4 did not fit the T. rex growth curve model.

facts.statement: A 2026 study indicates that Tyrannosaurus had foot-strike patterns similar to those of ostriches.
facts.quote: A study on the locomotion of Tyrannosaurus, indicative of similarity of foot-strike patterns to those of the ostrich, is published by Boeye et al. (2026).
